title: Open Addressing
summary: Hash tables that keep entries directly in the array - linear probing, why erasing needs tombstones (or backward-shift deletion), primary clustering and the expected probe counts, quadratic probing and double hashing, keeping the load factor below about 0.7, Robin Hood hashing, and power-of-two tables with a mixing step.

cards.q: In linear probing, why can't erase simply mark the slot empty?
cards.a:
Searches stop at the gap and miss later keys

A key that was pushed past this slot is found by probing through it. Searches stop at the first empty slot, so a hole breaks every probe sequence that ran through it.

cards.q: An open-addressing table has load factor 0.9. What happens?
cards.a:
Misses and inserts take about 50 probes each

With linear probing, probe counts grow like 1/(1-α)²; real tables rehash well before this.

cards.q: Why do many fast hash tables prefer linear probing despite primary clustering?
cards.a:
Neighbouring slots share cache lines

A few extra probes in the same cache line cost almost nothing: memory access, not probe count, dominates the cost on modern hardware.
